The short answer is no. Antibody tests usually test for the presence of two antibodies, like IgG and IgM, but these are not specific only to the SARS-CoV-2 virus, but are non-specific for the S and N proteins of the Corona viruses, and even other viruses.

Antibody tests have to be used as part of a fuller picture of diagnostic measures. Symptomology is still the most significant one. Of course, swab/PCR test is another step that would be more specific to the actual genetic material in Covid-19, but that comes with its own questions.

The issue with antibodies is not just the cross-reaction of the antibodies with similar proteins in the cold or influenza viruses, it's also that tests become a lot more successful many weeks out from your experiencing an infection. So in theory, waiting several months after a flu season (for example) would mean the most people had the most antigens to that virus, so testing for antigens (if you didn't know what the results meant) would make it seem like the virus was at its worst months after it had actually impacted the public.

Antigens are a delayed response, and usually they only really amplify to consistent levels in the blood if you are being regularly exposed to the contagion. They just aren't a good diagnostic tool in the sense I'm seeing the data being used in the media.

I hear what you're saying, but two points:

1. When source code is open to the public, it provides as much of a check-and-balance, I believe, as can reasonably be applied. Most (or maybe even all) may not read all the source, but the possibility being there certainly gives people reason to think twice, as there is the chance of being detected/caught. This is even more the case, perhaps, when those intending to compromise browser security are those in best position to exploit the vulnerability on a large scale -- i.e., big tech, or government (or both).

2. If you know what you're looking for, there are specific areas of (e.g., web browser) source, that are far more likely to contain vulnerabilities. And once those parts are verified, it is relatively less daunting -- perhaps manageable to periodically check those areas for functional changes.

I do agree, it is always possible for open source software to have exploits, however I would much rather use an open-source browser than a closed one -- especially from companies that have clearly demonstrated they are not the least interested in safeguarding user privacy, and in fact are harvesting every aspect of user data possible, and using it internally, and/or selling it to third parties.

The theory checks out, but in practice the Chrome engine is mostly developed by people with a close relationship to Google and being the core of so many browsers, it's also the most attractive target for attackers. Who could disguise as developers and slip things in. Open source doesn't really have background checks and vetting for new contributors. So I think it's a better idea to use other projects, too.
